beats.intro: Chapter nine, lesson one. Energy flow, catabolism and redox. [[sun]]Sunlight pours down onto a leaf. [[leaf]]The leaf captures some of that light and stores it as the chemical energy of sugar. [[heat]]And sooner or later, every living thing lets that energy go as heat, which never comes back. Energy flows through an ecosystem: in as light, out as heat. [[cell]]Now follow an animal that eats the leaf. Its cells must turn the energy in food into something they can spend. [[mito]]Zoom in further, and inside the cell we find the mitochondrion, where most of that work happens. This chapter follows that process, one step at a time.
beats.cycle: [[photo]]Plants and other producers use light energy to build organic molecules and oxygen out of carbon dioxide and water. [[resp]]Cellular respiration, in the mitochondria, takes those organic molecules and oxygen, and breaks the molecules down. [[back]]What is left over is carbon dioxide and water, and these go straight back to photosynthesis. So matter goes round in a circle. [[atp]]The breakdown generates A T P, the molecule that powers most cellular work. [[heat2]]And part of the energy escapes as heat. Matter cycles, but energy only flows through, one way.
beats.kinds: [[cat]]Breaking organic molecules down is a catabolic pathway, and it is exergonic: it releases free energy. [[ox]]It yields that energy by oxidizing the fuel. In a moment we will see exactly what that word means. [[three]]There are three ways to do it. Fermentation is a partial breakdown of sugar, and it happens without oxygen. [[aero]]Aerobic respiration consumes organic molecules and oxygen, and yields A T P. [[anaer]]Anaerobic respiration is similar, but it consumes some compound other than oxygen. [[term]]The words cellular respiration cover both kinds of respiration, but they are often used to mean the aerobic one. That is the one we will follow.
beats.equation: [[fuel]]Cells can burn carbohydrates, fats and proteins, but we will trace just one fuel: glucose. [[eq]]One glucose plus six oxygen makes six carbon dioxide and six water, plus energy. [[count]]Count the carbons: six in the glucose, six in the carbon dioxide. Nothing is lost, only rearranged. [[energy]]The energy leaves as A T P and as heat. Cells never do this in one jump. Later lessons show how it is spread over many small steps.
beats.q1: Quick check. Where do the six carbons of glucose end up?
beats.redox: [[redox]]How does breaking down glucose release energy? Through redox reactions, short for oxidation and reduction. These are reactions that move electrons from one substance to another. [[na]]Take a sodium atom and a chlorine atom. [[xfer]]Sodium hands one electron to chlorine. [[oxid]]Losing electrons is oxidation, so sodium is oxidized, and becomes a sodium ion. [[red]]Gaining electrons is reduction, so chlorine is reduced, and becomes a chloride ion. Its charge drops, from zero to negative. [[agents]]The electron donor is called the reducing agent, because its electrons reduce the other substance. The electron receptor is called the oxidizing agent. Here sodium is the reducing agent, and chlorine the oxidizing agent. [[pair]]Notice that the two always happen together. One substance's loss is the other's gain.

beats.methane: [[ch4]]Not every redox reaction hands electrons over completely. Some only shift how electrons are shared in covalent bonds. Burning methane is one: methane plus two oxygen makes carbon dioxide and two water, plus energy. [[shift]]In methane, carbon shares its electron pairs fairly evenly with hydrogen. In carbon dioxide, the shared pairs sit closer to oxygen, because oxygen is very electronegative. [[ox2]]So carbon has lost its share of electrons: it is oxidized. [[red2]]And oxygen has gained a share: it is reduced. [[ag2]]Methane is the reducing agent, and oxygen is the oxidizing agent. [[link]]Glucose burns the same way. Its carbons are oxidized to carbon dioxide, oxygen is reduced to water, and that shift in electron sharing is the energy we are after.
beats.map: [[map0]]Let's sketch where this chapter is going. [[gly]]First, glycolysis, in the cytosol, splits glucose into pyruvate. [[mito2]]Then, inside the mitochondrion, comes pyruvate oxidation, the citric acid cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation. [[elec]]Electrons are carried on shuttles called N A D H and F A D H two, and they run over to the last stage. [[atpm]]A T P comes out of glycolysis, the cycle and the last stage, and the last stage makes the most. [[next]]This is our respiration map. Every lesson in this chapter opens here, with one part lit up.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[s1]]Energy flows into an ecosystem as light and out as heat, while matter cycles between photosynthesis and respiration. [[s2]]Catabolic pathways release energy by oxidizing fuels, and glucose is our traced fuel. [[s3]]Oxidation is loss of electrons, reduction is gain, and in methane the loss is only a shift in sharing. [[end]]Now try the practice.
